design_detail: Systematic review with narrative synthesis (no meta-analysis) of deaths, and of injuries with medico-legal relevance, in police and prison custody linked to physical restraint, use-of-force devices and the label 'excited delirium' (ExD; the authors prefer 'acute behavioral disturbance', ABD). PubMed and Scopus, 1 January 2010 to 1 September 2025, English or Portuguese, reported against PRISMA 2009; earlier studies admitted from reference lists when 'frequently cited' or 'foundational', plus automated database suggestions, grey literature from official bodies, and two articles added during peer review. 116 included studies by the authors' count (62 rated good, 51 fair, 3 weak), spanning observational studies, case series and reports, forensic reports, experiments in healthy volunteers and animals, and systematic and scoping reviews; narrative, qualitative and opinion articles used as context. Presented as a predefined thematic subset of a broader review of deaths in custody. The review counts no deaths and pools no proportions.
can_establish: What the restraint-and-custody literature since 2010, as selected and summarized by these authors, says about deaths in custody: that 'excited delirium' has no validated diagnostic criteria and works as a diagnosis of exclusion, that autopsy and biomarker findings are non-specific, which mechanisms are proposed, which single-study figures exist, and what the authors recommend for investigation and certification.
cannot_establish: How often drugs cause or contribute to deaths in custody, how often restraint deaths are misclassified or missed in official statistics, or which mechanism operates in a given death: no deaths are counted, no drug proportions or concentrations are reported, the 116 included studies are not identified in the article, and the mechanistic conclusions rest on narrative selection weighted toward reviews from one author group and series of deaths selected on the outcome.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (review). PubMed and Scopus searched with combinations of keywords and MeSH terms, 1 January 2010 to 1 September 2025, English or Portuguese, no restriction by country or legal system; earlier studies from reference screening; automated database suggestions; grey literature and normative documents from international and national forensic, human-rights and public-health bodies; two articles added during peer review 'to broaden the epidemiological scope' (p. 2, Methods, 5th–7th paragraphs).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Population: people under the direct physical or legal control of police or correctional officers and not free to leave (street arrest, transport, interrogation, imprisonment) who were exposed to deliberate force or coercive measures (high-risk positions such as prone, mechanical restraints, conducted energy devices); routine administrative encounters excluded. Outcomes: deaths in custody of any cause, natural or non-natural, and restraint-related injuries needing forensic examination, medical documentation or judicial investigation. Included designs: observational studies, case series, forensic reports, experimental studies, systematic and scoping reviews. Narrative articles, qualitative studies, official documents, book chapters and reflective papers used as contextual evidence; editorials and commentaries on ExD used only for the conceptual and ethical framework. Excluded: letters without original data, duplicate publications, non-custodial populations except post-release analyses linked to custodial events (p. 2, Methods, 3rd–6th paragraphs).
sample.demographics: Not reported for the review as a whole. The review describes restraint-related deaths in the literature as predominantly in young or middle-aged men, often with obesity and psychostimulant intoxication, and reports over-representation of racialized minorities among deaths classified as 'legal intervention'; no counts are given (p. 3, section 3.1, 1st and 3rd paragraphs).
sample.attrition: Not applicable. Screening numbers are in the PRISMA 2009 flow diagram in the supplementary material, which was not among the files read.
sample.selection_effects: Selection is only partly reproducible: no search terms are printed, the date and language limits are not justified, pre-2010 sources entered by an undefined rule (for example Stratton et al., 2001; O'Halloran & Frank, 2000; Strote & Range Hutson, 2006; three book chapters), two articles were added at peer review without being named, and the article's 68 references (8 on methods) cannot account for 116 included studies, so readers cannot tell which studies support which statement. The authors state that the primary literature is overwhelmingly observational and retrospective and drawn from secondary sources (autopsy summaries, police use-of-force logs, civil-litigation records), mostly from high-income countries (p. 6, Limitations). Series of deaths are selected on the outcome, and the 229-death series is cited to papers including a study of civil-litigated cases (reference titles, p. 7). The review does not cite the 2018 systematic review of excited delirium by Gonin et al. (on the project's death-counting list).

exposure.measurement: Varies across cited studies and is not tabulated. Restraint position, compression, devices (conducted energy devices, spit hoods, vascular neck restraint) are taken from police logs, autopsy and investigation reports, litigation records, or experimental protocols in healthy volunteers and animals. Drug exposure appears only as psychostimulants (cocaine, methamphetamine) and phencyclidine 'frequently identified in toxicological analyses' (p. 3), with no proportions, specimens, test panels or concentrations.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: No amount or concentration of any drug is reported. The only restraint-duration figure is from one retrospective series (58% of 229 deaths within 1–5 minutes of starting prone restraint; p. 3).
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed. Intoxication is one of several interacting factors (with restraint, exertion, obesity, hyperthermia and heart disease) in the authors' model, but no study's toxicology is summarized; alcohol is not discussed in the text and appears only in the title of one cited Finnish study (ref. 7).

comparison.controls: None at review level. Comparisons cited from single studies: deaths against non-fatal use-of-force encounters in prospective police cohorts (low mortality reported), features of 'excited delirium' against conducted-energy-device exposure, prone against non-prone positions in operational data, healthy volunteers in restraint positions against baseline, and post-mortem computed tomography against autopsy (pp. 3–4).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable at review level. The cited death series rarely have pre-event health, drug-use or full toxicology data beyond what autopsy and records give, which the authors acknowledge (p. 6, Limitations, 3rd paragraph).

outcomes.instruments: Narrative synthesis by theme: epidemiological and clinical profile; proposed mechanisms; experimental and physiological evidence; conducted energy devices and other techniques; medico-legal investigation. Quality appraisal with NHLBI tools (observational studies), JBI checklists (case reports, qualitative studies, opinion articles), SANRA (narrative reviews) and PRISMA-ScR with JBI guidance (scoping reviews); study-level ratings in Supplementary Table 1, not read (p. 2, Methods, 9th paragraph).
outcomes.validity_norms: No appraisal tool is named for the volunteer and animal experiments; PRISMA-ScR is a reporting checklist, not an appraisal tool; the 'predefined quality thresholds' used to retain studies for the Results are not stated; quality is summarized only as 62 good, 51 fair and 3 weak (pp. 2, 6).
outcomes.operationalization: Death in custody: any death while under police or correctional control, natural or non-natural. 'Excited delirium' as each source used it; the review reproduces a ten-feature law-enforcement checklist (constant activity, violent or bizarre behaviour, 'superhuman strength', high pain tolerance, no fatigue, rapid breathing, profuse sweating, marked hyperthermia, unresponsiveness to police, being naked or inappropriately clothed) but adopts no definition and no criteria of its own. Drug involvement is not operationalized, and how drug findings were weighed in assigning cause of death is not described for any cited study.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Titles and abstracts were screened by two independent reviewers and full-text disagreements resolved by consensus; who extracted data and who rated quality is not stated (p. 2, Methods, 7th–8th paragraphs).

analysis.effect_sizes: None pooled; figures are cited from single studies. Finland: 12 restraint-associated deaths among 21,036 autopsies (0.06%; ref. 7). A retrospective review of 229 deaths: 58% within 1–5 minutes of starting prone restraint, and verbal respiratory distress (for example 'I can't breathe') documented in at least 20% before cardiac collapse (refs. 24, 29). Ventilatory decreases 'frequently exceeding 28–40%' in prone and hogtie conditions, as summarized in one review (ref. 36). 75 deaths temporally associated with TASER exposure: TASER considered a contributing factor in 27%, typically with physical restraint and intoxication (ref. 51). 944 applications of vascular neck restraint: immobilization in 92.6%, transient loss of consciousness in 23.7%, no deaths directly attributed (ref. 52). 46 investigative reports in Ontario: most deaths classified as accidental or natural (ref. 14) (pp. 3–4).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration is reported. The article calls itself a predefined thematic subset of a broader systematic review whose protocol also covered suicide and general mortality, but gives no registration number or citation for that protocol; two articles were added during peer review (p. 2, Methods, 2nd and 5th paragraphs).
analysis.selective_reporting: Results are statements without study counts, so the weight of evidence behind each cannot be seen. Evidence that does not fit the favoured model (low mortality in prospective use-of-force cohorts; operational data on prone positioning; volunteer experiments without hypoxia) is reported but discounted, while the retrospective death series and reviews that support it are not appraised in the text. The pooled analysis cited for the restraint-centred reading (Strömmer et al., 2020, ref. 32) is cited without its published critiques and the authors' replies (de Boer et al., 2023 and 2024; recorded on the project's card sc_strommer_2020).

interpretation_gap.results_show: A narrative account, without counts, of a literature dominated by retrospective death series, case reports, reviews and volunteer experiments: restraint-related deaths are described mostly in young or middle-aged men, often with obesity and stimulant intoxication; 'excited delirium' lacks validated criteria and specific autopsy or biomarker findings; volunteer studies of prone restraint show reduced lung volumes and more work of breathing without clinically significant hypoxia; one review of 229 deaths (cited to papers including a study of litigated cases) reports rapid collapse after prone restraint; most restraint deaths in one Ontario series of 46 reports were classified as accidental or natural; under-reporting in official vital statistics is asserted from one review without figures.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and conclusions state that deaths in custody are predominantly multifactorial, the Results that current evidence 'strongly favors' ventilatory compromise and metabolic collapse over stress-induced cardiac death (p. 3), the abstract that volunteer experiments 'should not be used to negate associated risks', and the Limitations that the evidence rests on 'a solid methodological foundation' (p. 6). The mechanistic preference rests mostly on reviews sharing one author (refs. 24, 29, 35, 36) and a pooled case analysis whose critiques are not mentioned (ref. 32); the same experimental literature is described as showing profound reductions in ventilatory capacity on p. 3 and modest ventilatory changes on p. 4; and the 'solid foundation' is a count of quality ratings from tools of different kinds, not an appraisal of the evidence for the causal claims. The Discussion also allows a catecholamine-driven arrhythmic pathway with stimulant intoxication in some deaths (p. 4, section 4.2; p. 5, section 4.3), which the Results section presents as weakened. The recommendations (complete autopsy with toxicology, independent investigation, avoiding prone positioning, replacing ExD with ABD) are expert judgments that the synthesis does not test.

timeline.event: Stratton et al., factors associated with sudden death of people restrained for excited delirium (ref. 34), a pre-2010 source admitted under the review's 'foundational' rule and cited for the restraint model (not read).
Vilke et al., defining review of excited delirium syndrome (ref. 11), cited for the clinical picture and for stimulants found on toxicology (not read).
Gonin et al., systematic review of excited delirium (on the project's death-counting list); not cited by this review.

Strömmer et al., pooled analysis of 168 published cases (ref. 32), cited as converging on a restraint-centred multifactorial reading; its critiques by de Boer et al. (2023, 2024) and the authors' replies, recorded on the project's card, are not cited here.
Steinberg, comprehensive review of prone restraint cardiac arrest (ref. 36), the main source for the PEA/asystole argument and the 28–40% ventilatory figure (not read).
Slocum et al., scoping review seeking inter-specialty consensus on excited delirium syndrome (ref. 62), cited for moving to descriptive terminology (not read).

Steinberg & Frugoli, review of mortality with in-custody prone restraint (ref. 29), and Steinberg, Patel & Frugoli, study of civil-litigated prone restraint deaths (ref. 24): sources for the 229-death figures and the under-reporting statement (not read).

replication.where_it_stands: Contested field. This review adds a 2010–2025 search but no counts, pooled estimates or reconciliation of the conflicting evidence, so it is a guide to sources rather than an estimate. How often deaths labelled 'excited delirium' are restraint deaths, drug deaths or both remains open. The review may be cited for the status of the ExD label (no validated criteria, not in DSM or ICD, used as a diagnosis of exclusion), for the non-specificity of autopsy and biomarker findings, for the single-study figures it quotes (as second-hand), and for the authors' recommendations on investigation; not for the frequency or causal role of drugs, nor for one mechanism dominating.

funding.funder: This research received no external funding (Funding source, p. 6).
funding.affiliations_note: First author: Department of Forensic Medicine, Faculty of Medicine, University of Porto; second author also National Institute of Legal Medicine and Forensic Sciences, Coimbra, Portugal (p. 1). AI-assisted tools are declared for translation, language revision and the Fig. 1 conceptual image, not for content, analysis or interpretation; the declaration speaks of a single author for a two-author paper (p. 6).

what_would_settle_it: A prospective, multi-jurisdiction register of every death in police and prison custody, with standardized recording of restraint position and duration, compression, devices used, initial cardiac rhythm, core temperature, blood gases, full toxicology with concentrations, and full autopsy by investigators independent of the custodial authority, compared with a register of non-fatal use-of-force encounters from the same jurisdictions (the authors themselves call for prospective multicentre data with standardized definitions, p. 5).

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (people under police or prison control exposed to force or coercive measures), interventions (restraint positions, mechanical restraints, conducted energy devices) and outcomes (deaths of any cause; medico-legally relevant injuries) are defined (p. 2), but there is no comparator and the aims (mechanisms, clinical profile, investigation practice) are not framed as PICO questions.
No registration or citable protocol; the review is described as a predefined subset of a broader review whose protocol is not cited, and two unnamed articles were added during peer review (p. 2).
Included and 'contextual' designs are listed but the choice is not explained, and primary studies are synthesized together with reviews that may contain them.

Two databases (PubMed, Scopus) with reference screening, automated suggestions and grey literature, but no search terms or strategy are printed, the language (English, Portuguese) and date limits (2010–2025) are not justified, and pre-2010 studies entered by an undefined 'frequently cited or foundational' rule. The supplement is described as holding the flow diagram and the quality table, not the search.

Two independent reviewers screened titles and abstracts, with disagreements resolved by consensus (p. 2). Studies added from reference lists, automated suggestions, the 'foundational' rule and peer review fall outside this process.
Who extracted the data, and whether in duplicate, is not reported.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: No list of excluded studies in the article; the supplement is described as containing the PRISMA 2009 flow diagram and Supplementary Table 1 (quality assessment), neither of which is a list of exclusions; the supplement was not read.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: The article has no table of included studies; the extracted items (authorship, year, design, quality, sample, interventions, findings) may be presented in Supplementary Table 1, which was not read.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: Tools named by design: NHLBI tools for observational studies (which ask about confounding and selection), JBI checklists for case reports, qualitative and opinion articles, SANRA for narrative reviews, PRISMA-ScR with JBI guidance for scoping reviews. No tool is named for the volunteer and animal experiments, PRISMA-ScR is a reporting checklist, the retention threshold is not stated, and study-level ratings are only in the unread supplement.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Not reported; funding is not among the extracted items (p. 2).

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The Limitations name retrospective designs, reliance on autopsy summaries, police logs and litigation records, and possible bias from ties between death-investigation systems and law enforcement, but then call the evidence a solid foundation on the strength of the quality counts. The mechanistic and multifactorial conclusions are drawn without considering selection on death and litigation or reliance on one author group's reviews, while volunteer experiments are discounted for indirectness.

Heterogeneity is named as the reason for not pooling. Conflicting findings (low mortality in prospective use-of-force cohorts and operational data on prone positioning; no hypoxia in volunteers) are explained by the favoured multifactorial model rather than examined for design differences such as selection on the outcome.
No quantitative synthesis; the Limitations acknowledge that publication bias cannot be excluded (p. 6).

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: No external funding; no conflicts declared (p. 6).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Provisional: item 8 can be judged only from Supplementary Table 1, which was not read; the overall rating does not depend on it. Four critical items are not met in the article itself: no registered or citable protocol (2), a search without printed terms or justified limits (4), no list of excluded studies (7), and no account of risk of bias when drawing the mechanistic conclusions (13); item 9 is met only in part. Under AMSTAR 2, more than one critical flaw gives critically low confidence. The review may be cited for what it reports the literature says about the ExD label, for the non-specificity of autopsy and biomarker findings, for the single-study figures it quotes (second-hand, with their primary sources named), and for the authors' recommendations on investigation; not for how often drugs are involved, for the cause of any death, or for one mechanism dominating.

key_findings.finding: Methods: PubMed and Scopus searched for 1 January 2010 to 1 September 2025 (English or Portuguese) under PRISMA 2009, with reference screening, automated database suggestions, grey literature, earlier 'frequently cited or foundational' studies, and two articles added during peer review; two independent reviewers screened titles and abstracts; results synthesized narratively because designs, settings (police vs prison), definitions of restraint, diagnostic criteria for ExD, legal frameworks and outcome classifications varied too much to pool.

The authors rated the 116 included studies as good (62, 53.4%), fair (51, 44.0%) or weak (3, 2.6%) and state that only studies meeting predefined quality thresholds were retained for the Results and Discussion; the thresholds are not given.

The review states that 'excited delirium' lacks validated diagnostic criteria in the official classifications (DSM, ICD) and specific biomarkers, is used in medico-legal contexts to explain deaths in custody, is criticized as deflecting attention from restraint and as racially biased, and, with no pathognomonic autopsy findings, is classified as a diagnosis of exclusion; the authors favour 'acute behavioral disturbance', keep 'ExD' when citing historical concepts and the terms of the original studies, and recommend replacing the label with it where possible.
key_findings.locator: Introduction, 3rd paragraph (p. 1), 4th–5th paragraphs (p. 2); section 3.2, 6th paragraph (p. 3); section 5, 6th paragraph (p. 5)

key_findings.finding: Drugs: psychostimulants (cocaine, methamphetamine) and phencyclidine are described as 'frequently identified' in toxicological analyses, citing a 2012 defining review and a 2009 book chapter; no proportion, specimen, test panel or concentration is given, and the review does not say how drug findings were weighed in assigning cause of death.
key_findings.locator: Section 3.2, 4th paragraph (p. 3); reference list, refs. 11 and 38 (p. 7)

key_findings.finding: Profile: deaths involving prone restraint described as predominantly in young or middle-aged men, often with obesity and psychostimulant intoxication, commonly with handcuffing and body weight on the torso; racialized minorities over-represented among deaths classified as 'legal intervention'. The 3rd paragraph also reports that features of 'excited delirium' were documented in a minority of use-of-force encounters, that an accumulation of features went with hyperthermia (ref. 30), and that police and prehospital literature uses a ten-feature checklist for the picture, so the label is applied to living people in policing and prehospital care, not only in death investigation (editors' reading). No counts are given.

Counts cited: population-level data from Finland, 12 restraint-associated deaths among 21,036 autopsies (0.06%); a retrospective review of 229 deaths in which 58% occurred within 1–5 minutes of starting prone restraint and verbal respiratory distress was documented in at least 20% before cardiac collapse. The review also notes that prospective studies in controlled settings occasionally report low mortality.
key_findings.note: Second-hand (refs. 7, 24, 29). The review does not say how a death was classed as restraint-associated or by whom; ref. 24, one of the two sources for the 229 deaths, is titled as a study of civil-litigated cases (p. 7), so those deaths were selected through litigation.

key_findings.finding: Under-reporting: citing one 2025 review (ref. 29), the authors state that large-scale investigations show persistent under-reporting of restraint-related deaths in official vital statistics, so forensic, police and open-source data must be combined to quantify them; no figures are given.

Classification: an analysis of 46 investigative reports in Ontario found frequent interplay between physical restraint and individual risk factors such as substance use or comorbidity, with most deaths classified as accidental or natural (ref. 14); the Introduction cites the same source for critics' view that ExD is used to classify restraint deaths as accidental or natural.
key_findings.note: Who classified the deaths (coroners or inquests) and on what evidence is not stated in the review.

key_findings.finding: Mechanisms: the review favours ventilatory compromise with metabolic acidosis ('prone restraint cardiac arrest') over stress-induced arrhythmic death, because terminal rhythms in prone restraint deaths are reported to be mostly pulseless electrical activity or asystole rather than ventricular arrhythmias (refs. 35, 36); the Discussion still allows that catecholamine surges with stimulant intoxication may precipitate malignant arrhythmias in some deaths and recommends recording the initial heart rhythm to tell the pathways apart.
key_findings.locator: Section 3.2, 1st–3rd paragraphs (p. 3); section 4.2, 6th paragraph (p. 4); section 4.3, 2nd–3rd paragraphs (p. 5)

key_findings.finding: Experiments in healthy volunteers: prone and weighted restraint reduced lung volumes and increased work of breathing without clinically significant hypoxia or major haemodynamic compromise; one review is cited for ventilatory decreases frequently exceeding 28–40% in prone and hogtie conditions; spit hoods produced no clinically significant changes in oxygen saturation or haemodynamics; in simulated encounters, intense exertion produced larger metabolic disturbances than conducted energy devices, chemical sprays or police dogs. The authors hold that volunteer data cannot be extrapolated to custody with agitation, exertion, obesity, stimulant intoxication and prolonged struggle.

Conducted energy devices: in animal models, repeated or prolonged discharges caused marked acidaemia and apnoea with rapid recovery in most trials and a low risk of ventricular fibrillation; in human volunteers brief discharges raised serum lactate only. In one series of 75 deaths that followed TASER exposure closely in time, those who died were mostly men with frequent cardiovascular disease and stimulant intoxication, and TASER was considered a contributing factor in 27%, typically with physical restraint and intoxication.
key_findings.note: Who judged TASER contributory (pathologists or the study's authors) is not stated in the review.

key_findings.finding: Investigation: conventional autopsy findings were often non-specific for distinguishing mechanical asphyxia from stress-related cardiac death or ExDS; post-mortem computed tomography showed sensitivity comparable to autopsy for major findings; superficial bruising was detected less often in people with darker skin and better with specialized dissection; deaths attributed to ExDS may occur without overt restraint or initially resemble homicide.

Biomarkers: HSP70 expression has been found in people with documented cocaine use regardless of any ExD diagnosis, so the review treats such markers as non-specific stress responses; it states that no single pathological or molecular finding establishes causality and that comprehensive toxicological analysis is indispensable for distinguishing intoxication from other mechanisms in deaths initially attributed to ExD.

Recommendations: timely, independent medico-legal investigation of every death in custody by experienced teams without functional dependence on the custodial authority, with complete autopsy, full toxicology and scene reconstruction (and documentation of initial heart rhythm, blood gases, restraint duration and position); review of restraint protocols with prone positioning avoided or kept brief; replacing ExD with ABD where possible; periodic independent audits.

Limitations stated by the authors: two databases only; publication bias cannot be excluded; heterogeneity prevents direct comparison; evidence mostly from high-income countries; primary literature overwhelmingly observational and retrospective, built on secondary records (autopsy summaries, police records of force used, records from civil litigation) that lack standardized clinical variables; ties between some death-investigation systems and law enforcement may bias causal interpretation and reporting of in-custody deaths.

reporting_issues.issue: The review reports 116 included studies, but the article has 68 references, 8 of them on methods (snowballing, review steps, NHLBI, JBI, SANRA and scoping-review guidance); at most 60 could be included studies, and some of those are textbooks, book chapters, a commentary and a philosophy-of-science paper.
reporting_issues.consequence: The included studies cannot be identified from the article, and most statements in the Results cannot be traced to the studies behind them; the list is presumably in the unread supplement.

reporting_issues.issue: Only studies meeting 'predefined quality thresholds' were retained for the Results and Discussion (p. 2), yet the thresholds are not stated and the Limitations count 3 'weak' studies among the 116 included (p. 6).
reporting_issues.consequence: It is unclear which studies were used and whether weak studies inform the conclusions.

reporting_issues.issue: The same experimental literature is described as showing 'profound reductions in ventilatory capacity' (p. 3, attributed to an uncited 'systematic evaluation of experimental data') and 'significant impairments' (p. 3, ref. 36, a single-author review that sets aside earlier readings of the changes as clinically modest), and then as showing 'modest ventilatory changes' (p. 4, refs. 46–47).
reporting_issues.consequence: The size of the ventilatory effect cannot be taken from this review; the primary experiments must be read.

reporting_issues.issue: The search window is 2010–2025, but many cited sources predate it (for example refs. 27, 34, 51, 53, 59, 60 and book chapters 6, 12, 38), admitted by an undefined 'frequently cited or foundational' rule; the two articles added at peer review are not named.
reporting_issues.consequence: Selection is discretionary and cannot be reproduced.

reporting_issues.issue: The statement that 'narrative reviews converge' on a multifactorial explanation of deaths attributed to ExD cites a pooled analysis of published cases (ref. 32) and a philosophy-of-science article (ref. 65), not narrative reviews.
reporting_issues.consequence: The claimed convergence rests on two sources of other kinds; the pooled analysis has published critiques that the review does not mention.
